rules.title: Fair Chance in Housing Act: limits on criminal history screening and drug testing of rental applicants
rules.requirement: A landlord may not ask about your criminal record, orally or in writing, until after it has made you a conditional offer. After the offer it may consider only certain convictions within set lookback periods, and it must do an individualized assessment before withdrawing the offer. A landlord also may not require a drug or alcohol test or ask for your consent to get records from a drug treatment facility.
rules.key_value: No criminal record inquiry before conditional offer; lookback limits of 6 years (1st degree), 4 years (2nd/3rd degree), 1 year (4th degree)
rules.coverage_conditions: Housing providers offering rental dwelling units in New Jersey, except units in owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units.
rules.exemptions: Dwelling units in owner-occupied premises of not more than four units. Before a conditional offer, a provider may still ask about a methamphetamine-production conviction on federally assisted housing premises and about lifetime sex offender registration. Arrests without conviction, expunged, pardoned, vacated or sealed records, and juvenile adjudications may never be considered.
rules.citation: N.J.S.A. 46:8-52 et seq. (Fair Chance in Housing Act, P.L. 2021, c.110), incl. §§ 46:8-55, 46:8-56, 46:8-60
rules.penalty: Civil penalty through a Division on Civil Rights complaint: up to $1,000 for a first violation, up to $5,000 for a second within 5 years, and up to $10,000 for a third or later within 7 years. The Director may also order the application fee returned and up to $1,000 paid to the applicant.

exemption_tests.description: Unit in owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units

rules.reason: Merged three partial records (§§ 4, 5 and 9) from the official text of the same Fair Chance in Housing Act.

rules.title: Law Against Discrimination: no refusal to rent based on source of lawful income
rules.requirement: A New Jersey landlord may not refuse to rent to you, or treat you differently, because of where your lawful income or rent money comes from (for example, a Section 8 voucher) or because of other protected traits. You can file a free complaint with the Division on Civil Rights within 180 days, or sue in Superior Court within two years.
rules.key_value: Source of lawful income or rent payment (e.g., Section 8 vouchers) may not be a basis for denial
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies statewide to rentals of residential real property, except where an exemption applies.
rules.exemptions: Rental of one apartment in a two-family dwelling where the owner lives in the other unit; rental of rooms in a one-family dwelling occupied by the owner or occupant; single-sex residences; religious organizations preferring persons of the same religion.
rules.penalty: Fines up to $10,000 for a first offense (N.J.S.A. 10:5-14.1a), plus damages. Remedies come through a Division on Civil Rights complaint (within 180 days) or a Superior Court action (within two years).
